rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation while preserving useful selectivity information. This should show whether compounds are unretained early, elute during the gradient, or are still pushed to the high-organic hold.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only lever is reducing t_last below 10 min; shorten the gradient and raise temperature to compress the chromatogram while keeping the wide window that already worked. This tests how much time can be removed before the closest mid-run pair starts to approach the 1.5 resolution threshold.

The limiting pair collapsed at higher temperature and shorter tG, so keep T at 50 C for speed but make the gradient shallower to recover resolution while aiming to stay under 10 min. This directly tests whether the critical pair is mainly slope-sensitive under the faster temperature condition.

The critical pair is clearly temperature-sensitive and was well resolved at 40 C but not at 50 C, so step temperature down while keeping the faster 14 min gradient that gave the best time. This should probe whether a small drop in T restores enough selectivity to keep the last peak under 10 min and improve CRF.

The close pair deteriorates as temperature rises, so return to 40 C where all pairs were resolved and keep the shorter 14 min gradient to see if this combination preserves full resolution while still keeping the last peak near the 10 min target. This isolates temperature as the main driver of the critical selectivity.

At 40 C the only remaining loss is the (6,7) pair, so make the gradient slightly shallower to try to push that pair above R=1.5 while keeping the last peak close enough to 10 min for a net gain. A 2 min increase is the smallest slope change available and should be near the optimum tradeoff.

The elution window is much narrower than 0.05–0.95, and trimming the high-organic end should make the effective gradient shallower in the region where all peaks elute, potentially improving the critical 6/7 pair without lengthening the run. This tests whether narrowing the phi window beats simply extending tG.

The narrower high-end window improved the score, so trim phi1 one more step to further flatten the effective slope around the clustered mid-eluting peaks while trying to keep t_last under 10 min. This is the most promising way to lift the 6/7 pair above 1.5 without paying a time penalty.

The best region is around phi1 0.85–0.90 and T 40 C, but the 6/7 pair looks highly temperature-selective; a modest increase to 45 C may move t_last well under 10 min, so compensate with a slightly longer and narrower gradient to try to preserve or improve that critical resolution. This probes whether a balanced shift in T and slope can beat the current best CRF of 0.989.

Temperature increases consistently hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so stay at 40 C and combine the narrower 0.90 window with the slightly longer 16 min gradient. This should be the cleanest test of whether we can push 6/7 above 1.5 while keeping the time penalty modest enough to beat or match the current best.

The current optimum appears to be a boundary between speed and the 6/7 resolution threshold, so shorten tG one step at the best temperature/window to see whether the time gain outweighs the expected small loss in the critical pair. This brackets the local optimum around the strong performer at 0.05–0.90, 14 min, 40 C.

The 6/7 pair is strongly temperature-sensitive in the favorable direction at lower T, and the current best method is already under 10 min, so a 5 C drop may improve selectivity enough to reach full resolution with only a small time increase. This is the most direct way to try for CRF 1.000.

The earliest peak is still well retained, so raising phi0 one step should trim dead early gradient space and slightly compress the whole run without changing temperature, which is clearly critical for selectivity. This tests whether shifting the window upward can keep the last peak below 10 min while preserving the near-optimal resolution pattern around the critical pair.

The upward-shifted window improved both speed and the critical pair, so trim phi1 one step to further flatten the gradient across the actual elution zone while staying near the current optimum. This is the most plausible path to push the 6/7 pair over R=1.5 and reach CRF 1.000.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the only useful next step is to find a faster method that still retains CRF 1.000. Shortening tG by one step at the winning phi window and temperature tests whether we can keep every pair at R>=1.5 while pulling the last peak safely below 10 min.

Since shortening tG lost full resolution, keep the winning 14 min slope time and trim phi1 one more step to see whether a slightly narrower gradient window can preserve R>=1.5 while pulling t_last just below 10 min. This is the best chance to keep CRF at 1.000 with a cleaner time margin.

We already have a CRF 1.000 method, so the only remaining upside is finding another 1.000 condition with more margin on the last peak; raising T could pull t_last below 10 min if selectivity survives. This checks whether the winning phi window is robust enough to tolerate a small temperature increase without losing the critical 6/7 resolution.

With temperature ruled out, the remaining unexplored way to gain time without steepening the active gradient too much is to shift the whole window upward by raising phi0. This tests whether trimming more low-organic dead space can keep the critical pair resolved while moving the last peak safely below 10 min.

Injection 18 achieved CRF 1.000 with better time margin, so push phi0 up one more step to see whether we can further reduce retention while keeping the critical 6/7 pair above 1.5. This is the logical boundary test for a faster equally optimal method.

Since raising phi0 to 0.20 made the critical pair fall below 1.5, stay at the successful 0.15 start and now test whether a shorter tG can still maintain full resolution with the extra selectivity margin already gained. This is the best remaining route to a faster CRF 1.000 method.

At phi0 0.15 and tG 14 we have full resolution with some margin, so a modest decrease in phi1 is worth testing as a possible way to rebalance the window and perhaps preserve full resolution while improving or at least maintaining speed. This explores the remaining adjacent window around the winning condition without changing the temperature-sensitive selectivity.

To map the local optimum around the successful phi0 0.15 condition, test the symmetric higher phi1 neighbor; this may slightly reduce t_last while showing whether the critical pair remains above the 1.5 threshold. It completes the key window bracket around the current best without altering the strongly temperature-dependent selectivity.

The 0.15–0.80 window gave the largest local resolution margin, so it is the best platform to test one last faster method by shortening tG. This checks whether the extra margin can absorb the steeper slope and still preserve CRF 1.000 with a shorter run.

With two injections left and two 1.000 methods already secured, use one to probe a different high-speed region: a slightly shallower gradient may offset the strong loss of 6/7 selectivity at 45 C while giving a last peak near or below 10 min. If this fails, the final injection can still be used for one last local boundary test around the winning 40 C conditions.

For the final shot, test the one remaining nearby condition most likely to preserve full resolution while moving the last peak just under 10 min: the narrow 0.10–0.80 window gave the largest 6/7 margin, so lengthening tG may convert that margin into a second fast CRF 1.000 method. This is the best untried local boundary around the winning 40 C region.
